title: Binary Operations
body:
The bitwise operations: they treat a value as a row of independent bits rather than as a
number. Each output bit depends only on the input bits in the same column, which is what
makes them one gate deep and effectively free in the [[ALU]].

| Op | 68000 | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| AND | `and` | 1 only where both are 1 |
| OR | `or` | 1 where either is 1 |
| XOR | `eor` | 1 where they differ |
| NOT | `not` | flip every bit |

The three idioms you actually use them for, all with a **mask**, a constant whose 1 bits
mark the positions you care about:

```
and.b   #%0000_1111,d0    ; clear   - keep the low nibble, zero the rest
or.b    #%1000_0000,d0    ; set     - force bit 7 on, leave the others
eor.b   #%0010_0000,d0    ; toggle  - flip bit 5 (this is the ASCII case flip)
btst    #3,d0             ; test    - is bit 3 set? answer lands in Z
```

Masking is how you read a device's [[Status Register]]: the register packs several unrelated
flags into one byte, and `and` with a one-bit mask is how you ask about just one of them.

## Shifts

Shifting moves bits sideways and is the cheap way to multiply or divide by powers of two.

| 68000 | Name | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `lsl` / `lsr` | logical shift | vacated bits filled with 0 |
| `asl` / `asr` | arithmetic shift | right shift copies the sign bit in |
| `rol` / `ror` | rotate | bits shifted out come back in the other end |

`lsl #1` doubles; `asr #1` halves a *signed* value correctly, where `lsr #1` would turn a
negative into a large positive by dropping the sign. That distinction is the entire reason
both exist, and it comes straight out of [[Complements]].

## Logical versus bitwise

C has both, and confusing them is a standard bug: `&` is per-bit, `&&` is the whole-value
truth test described in [[Boolean Representation]]. `1 & 2` is 0; `1 && 2` is true. In
assembly there is only the bitwise kind, and truth testing is done by setting the
[[Status Bits]] and branching.
